The central impedance-control problem is to learn both a kinematic reference and task-phase-dependent compliance without manually specifying which Cartesian axes should be stiff or compliant.\",\r\n  \"method_or_mechanism\": \"VICES augments the policy action with the parameters of a dynamically consistent end-effector impedance controller. The controller computes desired operational-space accelerations from pose error and end-effector velocity, uses the robot kinematic and dynamic models and the operational-space inertia matrix to obtain an end-effector wrench, and maps that wrench to joint torques through the transpose of the current Jacobian. Policies run at 20 Hz, controllers update and send joint-torque commands at 500 Hz, and consecutive policy actions and controller parameters are linearly interpolated. PPO is used for the reported action-space comparison.\",\r\n  \"content_summary\": \"The paper compares joint torque, velocity, position, joint variable impedance, fixed end-effector impedance at several gain levels, and VICES. Under an added energy objective, VICES was the only tested end-effector action space reported to improve energy efficiency consistently while preserving task performance; medium- and high-fixed-impedance policies became unstable, while joint-space variable impedance showed larger energy reduction partly because its initial solution was faster and more energy intensive. It defines impedance control as commanding a physically realizable dynamic relation between conjugate endpoint motion and force variables, rather than commanding position or force alone. Position, velocity, or force commands alone do not determine this exchange. The paper therefore reframes manipulation control around the behavior exposed at the endpoint interaction port, with effort and flow represented by force and motion or velocity. Free motion and pure kinematic constraints are treated as limiting cases within the broader dynamic-interaction problem.\",\r\n  \"method_or_mechanism\": \"The causal classification distinguishes admittances, which accept force and produce motion, from impedances, which accept imposed motion and produce force; the distinction is fundamental for nonlinear systems. Since inertial and constrained environments can consistently be represented as admittances, physical compatibility motivates commanding the manipulator as an impedance. For direct software implementation, a desired endpoint stiffness F=K(X0−X) is mapped to actuator torque through forward kinematics X=L(θ) and virtual work, T=J(θ)^T F. A desired endpoint force–velocity relation is implemented analogously as T=J(θ)^T B(J(θ)ω). These laws need neither inverse kinematics nor Jacobian inversion and allow nonlinear endpoint relations. The paper also describes masking the manipulator's true dynamics to impose simpler apparent endpoint inertia, while emphasizing that physical inertia cannot be eliminated. As an indirect implementation, kinematic redundancy changes the configuration-dependent endpoint mobility W(θ)=J(θ)Y(θ)J(θ)^T, allowing mechanical modulation of apparent inertial behavior without relying solely on feedback. Component impedances, including target-attractive and obstacle-repulsive potential fields, are added because the coupled admittance sums applied forces.\",\r\n  \"content_summary\": \"The paper introduces impedance control as a unified framework for free motion, kinematically constrained motion, and energetic interaction. Its core move is from controlling endpoint vectors to controlling the relation between endpoint force and motion. It argues that causal compatibility matters: a constrained inertial environment is naturally an admittance, so the robot should expose an impedance. Endpoint stiffness and damping can be imposed with commanded actuator torques, measured actuator positions and velocities, forward kinematics, and Jacobian-transpose mapping. This avoids solving inverse kinematics and supports redundant or nonsquare Jacobians without pseudoinverse control. Inertia requires separate care: simple stiffness and damping laws omit inertia, friction, and gravity, and no realizable controller can remove physical inertia, although apparent endpoint inertia may be modified through feedback or configuration. The endpoint mobility tensor provides a well-defined admittance-side representation even where an endpoint inertia inverse fails at singular configurations. The additive structure of component impedances permits target acquisition and obstacle avoidance to be designed separately and superimposed, including nonlinear repulsive fields. The authors report that one controller handled free-space avoidance of unpredictably moving objects and kinematically constrained motion in real time on a spherical-coordinate manipulator using one 8-bit, 2 MHz processor per axis. Adaptive control is discussed only as a complementary future strategy: fixed controlled impedance can handle rapid contact transitions while identification and adaptation optimize performance later.\",\r\n  \"synthesis_role\": \"Foundational problem-definition and implementation card for the development of robotic impedance control. Position-based impedance control retains the industrial robot's inner position servo and closes an outer force-sensing loop that modifies the commanded position to realize a diagonal target mass-damper-stiffness impedance. Its ideal target model can have an asymptotically stable in-contact equilibrium while the physical unilateral constraint is violated transiently by rebound. Stable transition therefore requires penetration to remain positive, equivalently contact force to remain nonnegative in the selected compliance direction. In the ideal second-order SISO model, positive nominal acceleration at contact, greater target damping, and higher target frequency support continuous contact; for constant-velocity impact, the minimum damping is determined from the derived critical-point equations. The reported key result is that the delay-free stability boundary depends on target damping ratio and the environment-to-target stiffness ratio, not on target frequency. High compliance against a stiff environment produces a large stiffness ratio and requires significant overdamping. Coulomb friction enters through the position-loop sensitivity and is argued to be negligible for a stiff industrial position servo and directionally helpful because it resists loss of contact. Delay has the opposite effect: delayed force information significantly increases required damping, makes natural frequency consequential, and is identified experimentally as a crucial cause of contact loss. The infinity-norm criterion is more conservative than the time-domain bound but easier to compute and incorporate model uncertainty. Experiments on a Manutec-r3 used an 8 ms computation cycle and maximum 8 ms force-sensing/computation delay, a goal 8 mm beyond a 60000 N/m environment, target stiffnesses from 250 to 8000 N/m, target frequencies from 0.5 to 8 Hz, and masses selected from 0.1 to 200 kg. Reported transition boundaries agreed closely with the delayed second-order model at 6-8 Hz and relatively low stiffness ratios; at 0.5-1 Hz, greater damping was needed. The 8 Hz setting approached the position-loop bandwidth and was discouraged for practical use. The conservative infinity-norm rule always prescribed more damping. The authors report lower minimum damping than earlier criteria, allowing faster response and smaller impact-force overshoot.\",\r\n  \"synthesis_role\": \"Transition-stability card that converts the early continuous-impedance idea into explicit design rules for establishing contact on industrial position-controlled robots. The IMC loop requires only desired mass, damping, and stiffness. Full robot dynamics compensation is replaced by time-delay estimation: Cartesian dynamics are partitioned into a chosen known inertia matrix Mbar_x times acceleration plus an unknown term H containing inertia mismatch, nonlinear dynamics, and interaction force. Assuming H is continuous or piecewise continuous and the delay L is sufficiently small, H(t) is approximated by the previous-step value Fu(t-L)-Mbar_x*x_ddot(t-L). The resulting torque command uses the Jacobian transpose, current desired impedance command, and one-step-delayed force and acceleration information. A recursive reformulation removes explicit real-time integration of the internal-model state. A diagonal forgetting-factor matrix attenuates accumulated quantization error in the recursive IMC feedback, while a first-order low-pass filter may be used in the TDE loop. In dynamics-based impedance control, model error enters through the desired impedance dynamics directly, so exact target behavior is fragile. In position-based impedance control, adjustable inner-loop PD gains attenuate model error, but the inverse inner-loop dynamics remain in the error channel and corrupt the commanded impedance. Instantaneous-model impedance control retains this contamination. The proposed IMC structure adds a parallel model identical to the desired impedance, producing a correction term based only on dynamics-estimation error. With no feedback delay, the derived reference-position error is zero even when model error is present. With discrete delay L, the response error becomes the target-impedance inverse multiplied by (1-exp(-Ls)) and TDE error, which attenuates slowly varying error without adding a foreign inner-loop impedance. TDE avoids full dynamics parameters but needs Mbar_x, the Jacobian, recent input force, and numerically estimated acceleration. The practical recursive implementation eliminates the internal model state, adds forgetting factors to suppress cumulative quantization error, and may filter the TDE signal. The L-infinity theorem assumes bounded desired trajectory derivatives and external force and requires the induced-norm mismatch between Mbar_x and actual Cartesian inertia to be smaller than a bound determined by the forgetting-factor matrix. Larger forgetting factors strengthen IMC correction but shrink the admissible Mbar_x stability region, exposing a remaining stability-versus-robustness tradeoff. Experiments use a 2-DOF SCARA-type robot at 1 kHz against an aluminum plate of about 150000 N/m. The task approaches the wall along y, moves 0.15 m along x while maintaining contact, and then holds. The desired impedance is 20 kg, 900 N s/m, and 400 N/m per axis, with damping ratio 5. Without payload, the proposed controller has the smallest free-space deviation, impact force of 57.6 N versus 70.2 N for position-based control, smallest contact-force fluctuation, and smallest impedance error; position-based control reportedly loses wall contact six times. Dynamics-based and instantaneous-model controllers have excessive free-space deviation and are excluded from further task comparison. With a 3.11 kg endpoint payload, the proposed controller again has the smallest position deviation, force fluctuation, and impedance error. Against a disturbance-observer implementation, the additional IMC loop improves results; below the 3.7 Hz motor torque-ripple peak, force PSD is reported at about 30% of the DOB controller's, while high-frequency fluctuation is limited by hardware torque ripple.\",\r\n  \"synthesis_role\": \"Robust-realization card in the development of impedance control. Consensus\r\n\r\n```json\r\n[\r\n  \"Impedance control is fundamentally a port-behavior problem; isolated tracking stability is insufficient for energetic interaction.\",\r\n  \"Impedance/admittance The discriminator learns a neural reward r_theta(o,a) that distinguishes expert from policy-generated observation-action pairs; the generator is the variable-impedance policy and is optimized by TRPO against this reward. In the force-action variant, the policy and reward act on a Cartesian feedback-force command. In the gain-action variant, the policy and reward act on impedance parameters, while the fixed feedback structure computes F_fb=-B dot(e)-K e. Peg-in-Hole outputs six diagonal stiffness values with fixed damping. Cup-on-Plate outputs six diagonal stiffnesses and a scalar d with B=d sqrt(K). \\\"db04e4a2ccce405a9f6c2870093a7ed8\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_sha256\\\": \\\"a08b5c73726ad1a38f2c4a541e0a263dd20e10a5a3e2529239d0ad8bdb12c826\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Buerger and Hogan propose a computational loop-shaping procedure for interaction controllers that separates robot-port performance from coupled stability, searches controller pole/zero/gain space, and constrains the search either by passivity or by a less conservative complementary-stability condition. Complementary stability models the expected human-arm environment as a bounded set and converts stable coupling with every member of that set into a robust-stability test using the small-gain theorem and structured singular value. On one screw-driven single-DOF rehabilitation-robot module, the selected low-frequency lag force-feedback controller reduced Coulomb friction from 10-20 N to below 0.5 N and apparent inertia from 6 kg to 1.2 kg while passing the reported spring, hard-block, and human-arm tests more robustly than tested natural-admittance alternatives. Force feedback can suppress friction and inertia but threatens coupled stability. Classical servo loop-shaping tools do not transfer directly because robot-port performance depends on robot impedance alone, whereas stability depends on the robot-environment port-function product, and controller dynamics are embedded nonlinearly in robot impedance. The concrete platform is one screw-driven linear module intended for rehabilitation robotics.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"method_or_mechanism\\\": \\\"The method defines a frequency-domain cost from deviation between actual and target robot-port impedance and separately imposes a coupled-stability constraint. For a chosen controller structure, a computational grid searches pole, zero, and gain; at each pole-zero combination it finds the largest admissible gain and displays a design surface. First, positive-real port impedance enforces passivity. Then complementary stability replaces the all-passive-environments requirement with a set of expected environments represented by a nominal port function plus bounded uncertainty. For human arms, a second-order mass-spring-damper model with bounded real parameter deviations is used. The robot is inverted to admittance form and structured singular value/small-gain analysis tests robust stability across that environment set. This permits selected nonpassive controllers when their destabilizing environments lie outside the modeled set.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The paper first explains why interaction design differs structurally from ordinary servo design. It then applies computational loop shaping to a linear single-resonance model of a screw-driven robot with handle force-sensor dynamics. Under passivity, the search finds low-frequency lag/PI force compensation superior to proportional control for friction rejection. Complementary stability uses bounded human-arm inertia, damping, and stiffness from prior literature and identifies both lag and high-frequency lead regions with lower impedance cost than the passive design; the implemented high-frequency lead design was precluded by force-measurement bandwidth. A 1 kHz lag controller was tested against springs, a hard block, and vigorous human-arm grasp. Model predictions were conservative, possibly because unmodeled Coulomb friction dissipated energy. The controller was compared with natural admittance control and gave the better reported stability-performance combination on this platform. The conclusion identifies extension to multi-DOF/configuration-dependent systems as unresolved.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"synthesis_role\\\": \\\"Represents an early explicit relaxation of universal passivity: controller design uses a bounded task/environment class to gain performance while retaining robust coupled stability for that class. The controller computes desired operational-space accelerations from pose error and end-effector velocity, uses the robot kinematic and dynamic models and the operational-space inertia matrix to obtain an end-effector wrench, and maps that wrench to joint torques through the transpose of the current Jacobian. Policies run at 20 Hz, controllers update and send joint-torque commands at 500 Hz, and consecutive policy actions and controller parameters are linearly interpolated. In free-space path following, most action spaces except direct joint torque and low fixed end-effector impedance completed all four via-points, so variable impedance was not required for basic task success. Under an added energy objective, VICES was the only tested end-effector action space reported to improve energy efficiency consistently while preserving task performance; medium- and high-fixed-impedance policies became unstable, while joint-space variable impedance showed larger energy reduction partly because its initial solution was faster and more energy intensive. In door opening, medium, high, and variable end-effector impedance approached 100% task success; fixed medium impedance learned faster because its initial gains suited the specified door friction, fixed high impedance incurred lower reward through excessive forces, low impedance could not overcome friction, and VICES converged to suitable gains rather than showing a unique final-success advantage. End-effector policies transferred better than joint-space policies from a simulated Panda to a simulated Sawyer, but performance still dropped because embodiment-specific joint limits and generated forces were not removed completely. VICES showed its strongest reported benefit in surface wiping: it converged faster, achieved higher reward and the highest wiped-area ratio, and applied a reported mean force of 28 N, whereas alternatives exerted excessive force or insufficient force to wipe. The best simulated VICES wiping policy was transferred without retraining to a real robot and succeeded in 8 of 10 trials. This transfer used visual input transformed by color segmentation into simulator-like images, robot pose and velocity, an operational-space controller with robot-model knowledge, no direct force sensing, and a payload-triggered stop. Earlier analyses often asked whether an already-contacting robot-environment interconnection remains stable, but not whether first impact establishes continuous unilateral contact without bouncing. The paper studies an industrial position-controlled robot commanded to a nominal position behind a stiff obstacle and asks which target impedance parameters prevent loss of contact while absorbing impact energy.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"method_or_mechanism\\\": \\\"The robot is linearized in Cartesian space around a nominal trajectory, with Coriolis and centrifugal effects neglected at low contact velocity and gravity assumed ideally compensated. The passive environment is modeled locally as a linear mass-damper-stiffness relation, then simplified to dominant stiffness. Position-based impedance control retains the industrial robot's inner position servo and closes an outer force-sensing loop that modifies the commanded position to realize a diagonal target mass-damper-stiffness impedance. Transition stability is defined pragmatically by positive endpoint penetration or nonnegative contact force after first impact. For an ideal position servo and SISO contact direction, the resulting second-order penetration dynamics are solved in time domain. Necessary and sufficient loss-of-contact conditions are obtained by locating the critical phase-plane point where penetration returns to zero, although controller synthesis requires solving transcendental equations; a conservative estimate yields a minimum target damping ratio. A frequency-domain alternative requires the coupled impedance to be positive real, and an infinity-norm small-gain criterion provides a simpler sufficient, conservative bound applicable to continuous or discrete systems and able to include delay and uncertainty weights. A retarded differential model explicitly represents force-information delay; its characteristic quasipolynomial must have all roots in the open left half-plane.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The paper sharpens impedance-control stability analysis by separating equilibrium stability from impact-transition stability. Its ideal target model can have an asymptotically stable in-contact equilibrium while the physical unilateral constraint is violated transiently by rebound. Stable transition therefore requires penetration to remain positive, equivalently contact force to remain nonnegative in the selected compliance direction. In the ideal second-order SISO model, positive nominal acceleration at contact, greater target damping, and higher target frequency support continuous contact; for constant-velocity impact, the minimum damping is determined from the derived critical-point equations. The reported key result is that the delay-free stability boundary depends on target damping ratio and the environment-to-target stiffness ratio, not on target frequency. High compliance against a stiff environment produces a large stiffness ratio and requires significant overdamping. Coulomb friction enters through the position-loop sensitivity and is argued to be negligible for a stiff industrial position servo and directionally helpful because it resists loss of contact. Delay has the opposite effect: delayed force information significantly increases required damping, makes natural frequency consequential, and is identified experimentally as a crucial cause of contact loss. The infinity-norm criterion is more conservative than the time-domain bound but easier to compute and incorporate model uncertainty. Experiments on a Manutec-r3 used an 8 ms computation cycle and maximum 8 ms force-sensing/computation delay, a goal 8 mm beyond a 60000 N/m environment, target stiffnesses from 250 to 8000 N/m, target frequencies from 0.5 to 8 Hz, and masses selected from 0.1 to 200 kg. Reported transition boundaries agreed closely with the delayed second-order model at 6-8 Hz and relatively low stiffness ratios; at 0.5-1 Hz, greater damping was needed. The 8 Hz setting approached the position-loop bandwidth and was discouraged for practical use. The conservative infinity-norm rule always prescribed more damping. The authors report lower minimum damping than earlier criteria, allowing faster response and smaller impact-force overshoot.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"synthesis_role\\\": \\\"Transition-stability card that converts the early continuous-impedance idea into explicit design rules for establishing contact on industrial position-controlled robots. In the outer loop, recursive least squares estimates each decoupled environment direction's stiffness and damping after the first-contact equilibrium position is recorded. A receding-horizon quadratic program selects motion and force references close to the user's desired references while enforcing estimated Kelvin-Voigt dynamics and kinematic/force bounds. In the inner loop, a dynamic compensator and sliding function define robust model-reaching control; a discontinuous term sized from known model-error and disturbance bounds forces the sliding variables toward zero, thereby recovering the target model.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The paper formulates rigid-manipulator Cartesian dynamics with bounded model, friction, and disturbance errors and a stable, single-contact Kelvin-Voigt environment. Theorem 2 shows convergence of the robust model-reaching sliding variable and realization of the target model when the robust gain exceeds the stated uncertainty bound. Experiments use a seven-DOF Franka Emika Panda with an ATI Nano25 sensor at 1 kHz; estimation also runs at 1 kHz and trajectory adaptation at 200 Hz. Four controllers are compared during contact with a deformable plastic surface and a stiffer surface. \\\"35534dcf890bbe6172eb43a09c4e062e1fbfc2ab269de216d3be307f13140f9c\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Fisac et al. present a least-restrictive Hamilton-Jacobi reachability supervisor that normally passes through an independently generated learning-policy action but overrides it with a robust safety action when the state reaches the certified-set boundary or Bayesian confidence falls below a threshold. Conditional on modeled disturbance-set coverage and regularity assumptions, value-function superlevel sets are robust controlled invariant. The paper considers fully observable deterministic continuous-time systems with partially known dynamics, compact control and disturbance sets, state constraints, an approximate model, and an unknown deterministic Lipschitz state-dependent disturbance represented through bounded sets and Gaussian-process confidence intervals.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"method_or_mechanism\\\": \\\"The maximal robust controlled-invariant subset of the constraint set is represented as the nonnegative superlevel set of an infinite-horizon HJI value function. A safe controller maximizes the worst-case directional increase of that safety value. The applied action equals the independent learning-policy action when V(x)>0 and, in the validation-enhanced version, local confidence exceeds a threshold; otherwise the safe HJ action replaces it. Independent Gaussian processes infer disturbance components from residual-dynamics observations and local posterior confidence tests whether the current bound remains credible between costly global HJ recomputations. Because performance is generated independently and conditionally replaced, the mechanism is a post-hoc least-restrictive supervisor rather than one joint performance-feasibility optimizer.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The framework combines robust HJ reachability with Bayesian online model validation. It precomputes a safe set and boundary policy under an approximate dynamics-error bound, lets an arbitrary learning controller act inside the safe set, and overrides it at critical states. Gaussian-process evidence updates a local confidence score so the framework can intervene earlier when observations undermine the assumed bound. Conditional invariance and local probabilistic results are supplied. Low-dimensional vertical-flight experiments show collision prevention during poor initial learning, confidence-triggered intervention between seconds-scale safety-set recomputations, and recovery from an unmodeled fan disturbance. The method depends on full-state feedback, approximate dynamics, valid disturbance coverage, and available HJ lookup tables; it does not address a jointly constrained impedance update or hard real-time fallback semantics.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"synthesis_role\\\": \\\"Partial cross-domain Source Mechanism analogue for confidence-triggered certified fallback and negative boundary evidence: it contributes uncertainty-aware supervisory intervention, but fails intervention-level isomorphism to RMC-JOINT-UPDATE-TIME-FEASIBILITY because nominal performance and safety remain separate and deadline totality is absent.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"development_link\\\": \\\"For RMC-JOINT-UPDATE-TIME-FEASIBILITY, the source shows how an arbitrary nominal action can be filtered through a certified state-dependent safety relation and how declining model confidence can trigger intervention. \\\"method_or_mechanism\\\": \\\"Replace individual contact-force feasibility with membership of the resultant six-dimensional contact wrench in a contact wrench cone computed from surface geometry. For rectangular support and linearly approximated friction cones, Proposition 2 gives equivalent closed-form inequalities: Coulomb bounds on the resultant tangential force, ZMP or roll-pitch bounds within the support area, and a coupled interval for yaw torque whose width contracts as tangential force or roll-pitch torque approaches saturation. Desired stiffness in the force direction is set to zero. Traditional AHI updates an accumulated compensation from delayed force error using a fixed rate sigma. DAHI replaces that constant with either a reciprocal or exponential function of absolute force error, absolute force-error derivative, tuning weights alpha/beta, and a positive limit term. Large transient error therefore produces a small rate; as error and its derivative shrink, the rate rises. Routh-Hurwitz analysis of the scalar spring-contact closed loop, after approximating an infinite delayed sum and e^{-Ts} by 1-Ts, gives the update-rate bound. A discrete implementation computes force-error difference, schedules sigma, integrates the impedance relation, and sends position commands every 4 ms.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"Analytical comparisons show HI has zero step error but nonzero ramp/sinusoidal dynamic error, whereas AHI reduces dynamic error as sigma grows but also decreases transient damping. Plane, slope, and sine-surface cases compare HI, AHI at sigma 0.01 and 0.05, and both DAHI schedules. The discriminator learns a neural reward r_theta(o,a) that distinguishes expert from policy-generated observation-action pairs; the generator is the variable-impedance policy and is optimized by TRPO against this reward. In the force-action variant, the policy and reward act on a Cartesian feedback-force command. In the gain-action variant, the policy and reward act on impedance parameters, while the fixed feedback structure computes F_fb=-B dot(e)-K e. Peg-in-Hole outputs six diagonal stiffness values with fixed damping. Cup-on-Plate outputs six diagonal stiffnesses and a scalar d with B=d sqrt(K). Positivity constraints make the instantaneous diagonal K and B positive definite. During transfer evaluation, AIRL does not directly deploy the training policy: the learned reward is fixed and forward RL reoptimizes a new policy under the changed dynamics or geometry. Behavior cloning instead directly transfers its learned action policy. The structural reason advanced for gain-action transfer is that a changed sign or magnitude of tracking error changes the resulting feedback force automatically, whereas an imitated direct force may remain inappropriate.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The paper recasts learning variable impedance from demonstrations as joint reward-and-policy recovery rather than pure action regression. Simulated expert data consist of 50 trajectories per task generated by designed variable-impedance controllers: a fixed tip-stiffness law that becomes configuration-dependent at the peg center of mass, and a three-phase Cup-on-Plate gain schedule that accelerates, switches, and approaches slowly. AIRL learns a reward and policy in either gain or force action space. In the training scenarios, all learned approaches broadly imitate the expert. Under changed peg tilt and smaller peg/hole mesh scales, gain-based AIRL reports the highest or near-highest success; direct force AIRL can push in the wrong direction, while impedance feedback reverses force when error changes sign. Under four changed Cup-on-Plate initial positions, gain-based AIRL has the lowest relative performance difference in three cases and trails constant gain in one. For hardware, 30 human demonstrations provide measured six-axis force/torque and state; gains are estimated by sliding-window least squares, AIRL training occurs in simulation, and policies are evaluated on the real FANUC. Gain-based AIRL and gain-based BC are similar at the training initial point, but at a shifted initial point AIRL reports 13.4 mm average and 10.8 mm final deviation versus BC's 48.5 mm and 17.0 mm. Force-based AIRL drives the robot outside the feasible workspace and cannot finish. These results support the gain action as a useful feedback-structured inductive bias, not a universal reward or stability guarantee.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"synthesis_role\\\": \\\"This paper moves learning-based VIC from direct policy optimization or imitation toward recovering a reusable objective from demonstrations and then reoptimizing impedance policies under changed task settings. A positive-definite target mass, damping, and stiffness define the desired impedance between reference acceleration, velocity, position error, and contact force. The controller combines a stabilizing feedback law, a strictly passive dynamic compensator with chosen gains, an intermediate state, and a feedforward learning input updated between operations by an iterative rule using an intermediate reference-model error. The repeated task has a reference trajectory, but successful learning is judged by whether the measured motion-force relationship matches the specified target impedance. This matters because unknown environment stiffness and contact position prevent prior derivation of separate desired force and motion trajectories. A within-trial feedback controller and strictly passive dynamic compensator provide stability, while a feedforward term is updated after each operation. The theorem gives sufficient convergence conditions through selected feedback and compensator gains and bounds on nonlinear robot terms; higher gains can satisfy the inequalities, and lightly damped targets or very stiff environments require higher controller gain because of larger overshoot. The method does not require force-derivative or acceleration measurement. In free motion, zero contact force makes convergence of impedance error also imply convergence of trajectory error. The same learning controller is retained across contact transitions. Hardware tests use a SEIKO TT3000 SCARA with one prismatic and two revolute joints, encoder-based position, differentiated velocity, an endpoint Lord force sensor, and a 244 Hz sampling rate. The repeated path includes free tracking, free-to-contact transition, compliant motion along a constraint plane, contact-to-free transition, and final free tracking. A steel ball reduces tangential friction. The first trial sets the learned input to zero and therefore provides feedback-only behavior. Across repeated operations, the reported impedance errors for all three joints decrease sharply, motion tracking errors decrease, and the contact-axis position error converges to a nonzero steady value consistent with impedance behavior under force rather than to zero. The paper considers robots whose motor and link coordinates are separated by compliant joints and seeks a desired stiffness-and-damping relation to external forces while leaving link-side inertia unchanged. The practical setting is torque-sensor-equipped DLR lightweight robots intended for compliant interaction and contact with unknown or passive environments.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"method_or_mechanism\\\": \\\"Both controllers use a cascade. The inner loop negatively feeds back measured joint torque and algebraically transforms the motor equation so that the original diagonal motor inertia B behaves as a selected smaller positive-definite apparent inertia Bθ. This does not make the torque-feedback controller itself passive; rather, the controlled motor dynamics together with torque feedback form a passive block that can be interconnected with the passive link-side dynamics. The first outer controller splits its input into a motor-position PD term and a motor-position-based quasi-static gravity compensation term. Its stiffness gain accounts for the series connection of controller stiffness and physical joint stiffness, and its gravity estimate is obtained from the inverse of the static motor-to-link mapping. The second controller defines l(q)=g(q)−Kθ(q−qd), constructs the corresponding inverse quasi-static mapping, and combines gravity and stiffness in a single potential-based term plus damping. This merged design enforces Kθ(q0−qd)=τext exactly at steady state for constant external torque. Neither controller can reduce the complete fourth-order flexible-joint dynamics to the desired second-order impedance exactly; higher inner-loop torque feedback only improves the approximation.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The paper formulates a reduced flexible-joint model with link inertia, Coriolis and centrifugal terms, gravity, diagonal linear joint stiffness, diagonal motor inertia, motor angles, link angles, and external link torques. Negative joint-torque feedback is interpreted physically as reducing apparent motor inertia, improving approximation of the desired impedance and damping elastic-joint oscillations without shaping link-side inertia. For the first controller, stiffness/damping and gravity compensation are designed separately. Its passivity proof decomposes the closed loop into passive motor-side and link-side subsystems, while Proposition 2 proves asymptotic stability in free motion under Assumptions 1 and 2 and global asymptotic stability only when the gravity-curvature bound holds globally. The separate construction is stable and allows desired positive-definite stiffness arbitrarily close to zero, but it does not generally realize the desired static stiffness relation exactly when gravity and nonzero external torque act together. The second controller merges gravity and compliance through a combined potential. Proposition 4 proves free-motion asymptotic stability under Assumption 3, global asymptotic stability when that assumption holds globally, and passivity from external torque to link velocity during interaction. It exactly realizes the specified static stiffness relation, while still only approximating the full desired dynamic impedance. The Cartesian extension adds restrictions from Jacobian singularities and redundancy: damping is positive definite only away from singularity, nonredundant stability is local, and redundant robots require additional nullspace behavior. Experiments used the Cartesian extension on seven-degree-of-freedom DLR Lightweight Robot II and III platforms. Human push-pull tests produced force-displacement behavior close to the desired low and high Cartesian stiffnesses. In a wooden-surface impact test, the system remained stable, a measured static stiffness of about 3882 N/m was close to the commanded 4000 N/m, and the authors report that high impact velocities were handled. Step-response tests with a known approximately 4.5 kg load showed response changes expected from leaving effective inertia unshaped. Earlier force-control practice could require the contacted surface or force sensor to be compliant, which excludes rigid workpieces or sacrifices endpoint positioning accuracy. The study addresses a task containing free motion, collision with a rigid constraint, sliding constrained motion, and both contact transitions, while seeking one controller that regulates motion and interaction force without detecting contact and switching modes.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"method_or_mechanism\\\": \\\"The paper treats the workpiece or kinematic constraint as a mechanical admittance that accepts force and determines motion, requiring the coupled robot to present the complementary impedance. The chosen target endpoint behavior is the second-order relation Fexternal = M x_ddot + B x_dot + K(x-x0), where x0 is a software-defined virtual equilibrium and M, B, and K specify apparent inertia, damping, and stiffness. Starting from an inertial robot model with controllable joint torque, measured external force, joint position, and joint velocity, the nonlinear control law uses the Jacobian and the endpoint mobility W=J I^-1 J^T to make the endpoint approximate the target impedance. It avoids inverse kinematics by commanding the virtual endpoint position directly and computing joint torques from forward kinematics and dynamics. In a simplified one-dimensional analysis, negative external-force feedback with gain G changes the apparent mass from Mactual to Mactual/(G+1); force regulation additionally depends on an assumed environment model, whereas the apparent-inertia interpretation does not. The target parameters may in principle vary with time, but this paper does not give an adaptation rule or stability proof for such variation.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The paper advances classical impedance control from a general interaction concept to an experimental contact-execution architecture. It argues that neither motion nor force alone captures contact mechanics: a constrained workpiece is an admittance, so the robot must be controlled as an impedance. It derives a nonlinear endpoint impedance controller for a torque-controlled inertial mechanism, with a target mass-damper-spring behavior and endpoint force feedback. The derivation identifies force feedback as changing apparent inertia and shows that conventional force-tracking conclusions require environmental stiffness and damping assumptions. The implementation uses a planar two-link, SCARA-like, low-friction, low-inertia direct-drive laboratory mechanism; joint positions are measured by potentiometers, velocities are digitally differentiated, endpoint forces by a two-axis force sensor, and torque commands are computed on a DEC LSI 11/23 at 9 ms per cycle, about 111 Hz sampling and slightly over 5 Hz effective bandwidth. The virtual endpoint travels at constant speed around a circle intersected by a rigid concrete barrier. With force feedback, the apparatus remained stable in free motion, impact, and sliding contact; its force and path histories followed the ideal target behavior within sensor-noise and apparatus limits. The barrier was treated as essentially rigid, the force-sensor stiffness was reported as 700 lbf/ft, and robot stiffness as 4.5 lbf/ft. Stability was reported across the achievable stiffness and viscosity range. Disconnecting force sensing did not destabilize this particular mechanism, but caused repeated bouncing and substantially worse force history after impact, separating stability from performance. No contact detector, guarded move, inverse kinematics, or controller-mode switch was used.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"synthesis_role\\\": \\\"Contact-transition and implementation card showing how impedance control became a single executable strategy for free motion, collision, and sustained rigid contact. \\\"46203e975191e8aa01e6fe8e820867e6ac96f19e7053f2ea97450df97d32fad9\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"claim\\\": \\\"The accuracy/robustness dilemma is the structural tradeoff that dynamics-based impedance control can reproduce a desired endpoint impedance accurately only when the robot model is accurate, whereas position-based impedance control attenuates model error through a high-gain inner position loop but allows the resulting inner-loop dynamics to contaminate the desired impedance and can even lose contact. The proposed method restructures the controller as an internal-model-control loop whose internal model is the desired impedance itself, then uses time-delay estimation to compensate unknown nonlinear robot dynamics from one-step-delayed input and acceleration. In the zero-feedback-delay idealization the IMC correction cancels dynamics-estimation error without inserting a competing impedance; with sampled delay, the residual impedance error is filtered by a factor proportional to 1-exp(-Ls), so accuracy is improved but not perfect. A conditional L-infinity stability theorem and 2-DOF SCARA experiments support bounded, more accurate and payload-robust behavior, but the method remains constrained by time-delay-estimation smoothness, sampling and sensor resolution, gain-region tradeoffs, acceleration estimation, and the tested single-contact setting.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"claim_locator\\\": \\\"Abstract and Section I; Section II-A-E, Eqs. 1-28 and Fig. 1; Section III-A-E, Eqs. 29-66 and Figs. 2-4; Section IV-A-D, Eqs. 67-73, Tables I-II and Figs. 5-12; Section V, Eqs. 74-77 and Fig. 13; Section VI; Appendix Stability Theorem, Eqs. 78-93.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"access_level\\\": \\\"full_text\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"decision_grade\\\": \\\"decision_grade\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"epistemic_status\\\": \\\"Full-text primary controller-design and experimental-comparison study. Direct dynamics-based implementation depends on estimated inertia, Coriolis, centrifugal, gravity, and friction terms and has no independent gain for suppressing model error; sensitivity is especially high for small desired stiffness and large desired mass. Position-based implementation improves robustness by commanding an inner position servo, but model error excites the inner-loop dynamics, which generally differ from the target impedance, degrading force-motion accuracy and potentially causing oscillation or contact loss. The paper seeks simultaneous accuracy, robustness to modeling error, and a simple implementation that avoids full online robot-model computation.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"method_or_mechanism\\\": \\\"The proposed architecture recognizes dynamics-based impedance control as an internal-model-control-compatible plant. A parallel IMC path uses the desired impedance inverse as controller and the desired impedance as internal model, so the difference between actual and model response feeds back an estimate-error correction. The IMC loop requires only desired mass, damping, and stiffness. Full robot dynamics compensation is replaced by time-delay estimation: Cartesian dynamics are partitioned into a chosen known inertia matrix Mbar_x times acceleration plus an unknown term H containing inertia mismatch, nonlinear dynamics, and interaction force. Assuming H is continuous or piecewise continuous and the delay L is sufficiently small, H(t) is approximated by the previous-step value Fu(t-L)-Mbar_x*x_ddot(t-L). The resulting torque command uses the Jacobian transpose, current desired impedance command, and one-step-delayed force and acceleration information. A recursive reformulation removes explicit real-time integration of the internal-model state. A diagonal forgetting-factor matrix attenuates accumulated quantization error in the recursive IMC feedback, while a first-order low-pass filter may be used in the TDE loop. The ideal no-delay algebra gives exact target impedance independent of dynamics-estimation error; the implementable delayed form leaves an error proportional to the delayed difference of TDE error.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The paper first formalizes the dilemma using a nonlinear multi-axis robot. In dynamics-based impedance control, model error enters through the desired impedance dynamics directly, so exact target behavior is fragile. In position-based impedance control, adjustable inner-loop PD gains attenuate model error, but the inverse inner-loop dynamics remain in the error channel and corrupt the commanded impedance. Instantaneous-model impedance control retains this contamination. The proposed IMC structure adds a parallel model identical to the desired impedance, producing a correction term based only on dynamics-estimation error. With no feedback delay, the derived reference-position error is zero even when model error is present. With discrete delay L, the response error becomes the target-impedance inverse multiplied by (1-exp(-Ls)) and TDE error, which attenuates slowly varying error without adding a foreign inner-loop impedance. TDE avoids full dynamics parameters but needs Mbar_x, the Jacobian, recent input force, and numerically estimated acceleration. The practical recursive implementation eliminates the internal model state, adds forgetting factors to suppress cumulative quantization error, and may filter the TDE signal. The L-infinity theorem assumes bounded desired trajectory derivatives and external force and requires the induced-norm mismatch between Mbar_x and actual Cartesian inertia to be smaller than a bound determined by the forgetting-factor matrix. Larger forgetting factors strengthen IMC correction but shrink the admissible Mbar_x stability region, exposing a remaining stability-versus-robustness tradeoff. Experiments use a 2-DOF SCARA-type robot at 1 kHz against an aluminum plate of about 150000 N/m. The task approaches the wall along y, moves 0.15 m along x while maintaining contact, and then holds. The desired impedance is 20 kg, 900 N s/m, and 400 N/m per axis, with damping ratio 5. Without payload, the proposed controller has the smallest free-space deviation, impact force of 57.6 N versus 70.2 N for position-based control, smallest contact-force fluctuation, and smallest impedance error; position-based control reportedly loses wall contact six times. Dynamics-based and instantaneous-model controllers have excessive free-space deviation and are excluded from further task comparison. With a 3.11 kg endpoint payload, the proposed controller again has the smallest position deviation, force fluctuation, and impedance error. Against a disturbance-observer implementation, the additional IMC loop improves results; below the 3.7 Hz motor torque-ripple peak, force PSD is reported at about 30% of the DOB controller's, while high-frequency fluctuation is limited by hardware torque ripple.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"synthesis_role\\\": \\\"Robust-realization card in the development of impedance control. full-state and observer-based adaptive neural impedance controllers for uncertain robot dynamics with actuator saturation. Under bounded smooth desired trajectories, bounded initial conditions, standard rigid-robot structural properties, bounded neural approximation, and explicit controller/observer gain inequalities, the paper proves uniform ultimate boundedness and convergence of impedance tracking error to a tunable neighborhood for both feedback structures. Simulations of a two-link robot moving in free space and sliding against an obstacle report smaller errors than a nonadaptive PD controller; full-state feedback performs slightly better than output feedback. The saturation residual, defined as applied saturated torque minus the unsaturated command, drives an auxiliary state whose dynamics are designed to absorb saturation cross terms in the Lyapunov derivative. Leakage-modified neural weight updates bound the estimates. For output feedback, a high-gain observer estimates the unavailable velocity/error state, neural basis functions are evaluated on estimated inputs, and the proof adds observer-error bounds to the adaptive-control Lyapunov argument. A robust sign term is chosen to exceed approximation residuals, with an alternative state-dependent bound suggested to reduce conservatism.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The full-state theorem derives a differential inequality of the form V-dot less than or equal to minus kappa V plus C, implying uniform ultimate boundedness and an explicit compact bound for position error when gain matrices satisfy positivity conditions. The output-feedback theorem adds a small-parameter high-gain observer and further gain inequalities to obtain the same qualitative result. Simulation uses a two-degree-of-freedom vertical-plane manipulator, a circular trajectory intersecting a fixed obstacle, and asymmetric unknown torque saturation of plus/minus 17 and plus/minus 15. A PD-only case shows substantial tracking error. State-feedback adaptive neural impedance control with 256 Gaussian nodes per approximator reduces the error, while observer-based control also tracks with slightly worse performance. Position, velocity, or force commands alone do not determine this exchange. The paper therefore reframes manipulation control around the behavior exposed at the endpoint interaction port, with effort and flow represented by force and motion or velocity. Free motion and pure kinematic constraints are treated as limiting cases within the broader dynamic-interaction problem.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"method_or_mechanism\\\": \\\"The causal classification distinguishes admittances, which accept force and produce motion, from impedances, which accept imposed motion and produce force; the distinction is fundamental for nonlinear systems. Since inertial and constrained environments can consistently be represented as admittances, physical compatibility motivates commanding the manipulator as an impedance. For direct software implementation, a desired endpoint stiffness F=K(X0−X) is mapped to actuator torque through forward kinematics X=L(θ) and virtual work, T=J(θ)^T F. A desired endpoint force–velocity relation is implemented analogously as T=J(θ)^T B(J(θ)ω). These laws need neither inverse kinematics nor Jacobian inversion and allow nonlinear endpoint relations. The paper also describes masking the manipulator's true dynamics to impose simpler apparent endpoint inertia, while emphasizing that physical inertia cannot be eliminated. As an indirect implementation, kinematic redundancy changes the configuration-dependent endpoint mobility W(θ)=J(θ)Y(θ)J(θ)^T, allowing mechanical modulation of apparent inertial behavior without relying solely on feedback. Component impedances, including target-attractive and obstacle-repulsive potential fields, are added because the coupled admittance sums applied forces.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The paper introduces impedance control as a unified framework for free motion, kinematically constrained motion, and energetic interaction. Its core move is from controlling endpoint vectors to controlling the relation between endpoint force and motion. It argues that causal compatibility matters: a constrained inertial environment is naturally an admittance, so the robot should expose an impedance. Endpoint stiffness and damping can be imposed with commanded actuator torques, measured actuator positions and velocities, forward kinematics, and Jacobian-transpose mapping. This avoids solving inverse kinematics and supports redundant or nonsquare Jacobians without pseudoinverse control. Inertia requires separate care: simple stiffness and damping laws omit inertia, friction, and gravity, and no realizable controller can remove physical inertia, although apparent endpoint inertia may be modified through feedback or configuration. The endpoint mobility tensor provides a well-defined admittance-side representation even where an endpoint inertia inverse fails at singular configurations. The additive structure of component impedances permits target acquisition and obstacle avoidance to be designed separately and superimposed, including nonlinear repulsive fields. The authors report that one controller handled free-space avoidance of unpredictably moving objects and kinematically constrained motion in real time on a spherical-coordinate manipulator using one 8-bit, 2 MHz processor per axis. Adaptive control is discussed only as a complementary future strategy: fixed controlled impedance can handle rapid contact transitions while identification and adaptation optimize performance later.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"synthesis_role\\\": \\\"Foundational problem-definition and implementation card for the development of robotic impedance control. For robot learning, the required path integral is approximated by repeated noisy policy rollouts; trajectories with lower generalized cost receive exponentially larger weights, and weighted exploration perturbations update policy parameters. A DMP with basis functions represents each joint reference trajectory. A second basis-function dynamical equation represents each joint's proportional-gain schedule KP,i(t). The joint torque is −KP,i(qi−qd,i)−ξi√KP,i(q̇i−q̇d,i)+Tff,i, so KD,i is coupled to KP,i rather than learned independently. Motion and gain parameters are optimized dimension-wise even though task cost couples robot degrees of freedom. The task implementations use simpler rollout costs: via-point studies penalize summed proportional gains, end-effector acceleration, and timed joint/task-space error; switch flipping uses a binary success terminal cost plus gain penalty; door opening uses remaining door angle plus gain penalty. PI² does not require explicit robot/environment dynamics for parameter updates, but uses trials from a common start state and user-selected policy, cost, exploration, gain bounds, and rollout counts. After contact, desired stiffness is set to zero only in the force-controlled direction, leaving a target mass-damper relation. An additive term representing environment velocity is updated each sample from delayed force error. The resulting scalar force-error dynamics produce an adaptive-gain upper bound through a Routh-Hurwitz calculation and step-input convergence through the final-value theorem. Tests include abruptly changing stiffness on a flat wall, a sinusoidal wall, a flat wall with triangular crack, and a burr/deburring case. A standard time-varying PD-plus controller changes the active motor- and link-side stiffness/damping gains online. Its motor-side work algebraically removes the gain-dependent power terms from the Lyapunov/storage derivative, leaving dot(V)=-dot(q_F)^T Xi_K dot(q_F). Positive definiteness of Xi_K is enforced through Xi_D=N-(1/4)K_DJ^T(D+K_DM)^(-1)K_DJ>0. This is an online counter-power/damping modification: it does not store and ration energy as an energy tank does, and it does not merely reject gain profiles through an offline stiffness-rate certificate. The desired continuous gain schedule is retained, subject to the PPC correction and feasibility conditions. Joint- and Cartesian-space forms are developed; contact-wrench thresholds ramp between low and high gains, and an LQR construction supplies diagonal full-state gains at selected operating points.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The paper first derives the energy-injection term caused by varying the active stiffness of a compliant-joint robot. It then introduces PPC, whose auxiliary torque cancels this term and related noncollocated full-state-feedback power terms. Theorem 1 gives a conditional global asymptotic stability result for free motion, and Theorem 2 gives conditional passivity at the interaction port. A Cartesian version and an extension containing modeled passive-stiffness variation and friction compensation are also presented. The implementation uses contact-triggered ramps between LQR-derived low- and high-impedance gains. On a Sawyer robot, the PPC-based variable Cartesian controller maintained the claimed storage-power inequality in the reported trials, whereas a variable version of a conventional controller could violate it. In a plastering-trowel smoothing task, variable impedance reduced the reported contact-force magnitudes relative to fixed impedance. A separate simulation held pre-impact velocity equal and reported lower impact force with VIC. Deliberate violation of the paper's stiffness and damping criteria on hardware produced oscillation and instability, respectively. These results validate the proposed structured controller and tested schedules, not arbitrary learned or discontinuous VIC laws.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"synthesis_role\\\": \\\"This paper marks a transition from offline restrictions on admissible time-varying impedance and energy-tank gating toward an explicit online power-cancellation controller for actively scheduled impedance on compliant/flexible-joint robots. It makes the stability bottleneck concrete: a variable gain profile is not sufficient by itself; its implementation must account for energy injected through the robot's elastic, motor-side, and link-side dynamics.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"development_link\\\": \\\"Relative to fixed impedance, PPC permits continuous online gain scheduling while retaining a passivity proof for a flexible-joint plant. A second-order filter driven by reference trajectory xr and measured contact force Pm generates xd, the trajectory whose close tracking realizes that impedance. Defining a weighted Cartesian error q=ė+Ke, the controller computes F=A(t)ẍd*+B(t)[ẍẋ]+f(t)+Pm+Kpe+Kve, where A, B, and f are direct adaptive counterparts of task-space inertia, Coriolis/centripetal, and gravity terms rather than estimates of a physical parameter vector. The final adaptation laws use proportional-plus-integral, e1-modification-like leakage terms driven by error magnitude and task signals. F is mapped to joint torque: T=JᵀF for nonredundant robots; for redundant robots, the underdetermined inverse of a torque-to-Cartesian-force map can use generalized inverses or augmented coordinates to satisfy secondary kinematic objectives.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"content_summary\\\": \\\"The paper contrasts indirect adaptive control, which estimates a linearly parameterized dynamic model, with direct adaptation of controller gains. Its architecture separates desired impedance specification from robot tracking and redundancy resolution. The filter requires only integration of a simple desired impedance model, especially simple for diagonal gains. The Cartesian controller is designed from a task-space robot model but assumes no detailed structure or parameter values beyond compatible dimensions and regularity bounds used in analysis. A Lyapunov candidate combines tracking errors with adaptive-gain errors. Bounded sensor error and bounded task-space terms yield a derivative inequality in which higher-order negative terms dominate lower-order positive terms, implying convergence to a compact set and global stability; increasing gains can make the residual tracking bound arbitrarily small in the continuous-time analysis. The authors additionally state that if task-space dynamics vary slowly relative to adaptation and force/torque measurement error is negligible, the tracking is asymptotic. Section 4 sketches a physically realizable joint-torque mapping and secondary-task use of redundancy. No numerical results, experimental setup, plots of performance, or contact-task trial are included; only an unshown simulation study is cited as work to appear.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"synthesis_role\\\": \\\"Represents an early move from model-dependent impedance realization toward online direct adaptation in Cartesian space: it adapts controller coefficients needed to emulate a fixed desired impedance rather than learning the desired impedance itself. learned optimizer itself.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"Compliance, low measured force, boundedness, passivity, safe-set invariance and human safety are distinct evidence claims.\\\",\\r\\n  \\\"Most modern results
